summary: A report on the March 1972 meeting at MIT where Vint Cerf and colleagues formed the Network Measurement Group to plan measurement experiments on the ARPANET. The group agreed to set aside a range of links, 159 through 191, for measurement traffic. Some links were for a host discard service, and others were for traffic statistics sent by the IMPs.

plainLanguage.summary: A group of researchers met and decided to measure how well the early internet worked. They set aside some special lanes just for test traffic so they could count and time it.

subtitle: Minutes of the 1972 meeting that set up a group to measure the ARPANET and reserved links for test traffic.

tldr.problem: Several ARPANET sites were measuring their own network and host behavior in different ways, with no shared plan.
tldr.mechanism: A group met at MIT, formed the Network Measurement Group (NMG), reserved links 159 to 191 for measurement, and agreed on a minimal set of per-host traffic counts and a report format.
tldr.outcome: The RFC records proposals and agreements for experiments (discard services, NCP statistics, traffic generators). It is a meeting report, and RFC 388 later updated it.

today: RFC 323 is a March 1972 report of a meeting, and RFC 388 updates it. It describes plans for ARPANET measurement, not a deployed protocol.

sections.title: The Network Measurement Group
sections.content:
On March 17, 1972, a group met at MIT project MAC to discuss plans to perform measurement experiments on the ARPANET. Eight people attended, and V. Cerf of UCLA/NMC was named Chairman of the NMG. The purpose was to discuss existing and planned measurements of network and HOST behavior.

The RFC is Cerf's report of what was discussed and agreed.
sections.plainLanguage: Some grown-up scientists met in a room to plan how to check whether the network was working well. One of them was put in charge of the group.

sections.title: Links Reserved for Measurement
sections.content:
After what the RFC calls a ridiculously long discussion, the group agreed to allocate links 159 to 191 for network measurement only (see RFC 317). Links 159 to 174 are HOST DISCARD: cooperating HOSTs receiving messages on these links throw them away without generating an error message. Links 175 to 190 are to be allocated as needed by V. Cerf. Link 191 is used by IMPs to send measurement traffic obtained from IMP statistics packages.

A HOST that wants to support the discard service should modify its NCP to drop all messages on links 159 to 174 without sending an error back to the source HOST. No connection is open on these links.

A separate PROCESS DISCARD was also suggested by C. Kline at UCLA, to study process-to-process behavior. It would wait for ICP on a well-known socket, but no socket number was proposed until a survey of well-known sockets is complete (see RFC 322).
sections.plainLanguage: They picked a row of lanes just for test traffic. Some lanes were like a bin where test messages get thrown away so nobody gets confused.

sections.title: NCP Statistics and the Report Format
sections.content:
Several sites had already instrumented their NCPs out of curiosity. Joel Winett at Lincoln Labs, for example, gathered per-connection statistics for local TELNET users, such as network connect time, NCP CPU time and a log of errors.

The group agreed on a minimal NCP instrumentation procedure. For a standard 24 hour period, each HOST counts, per remote HOST, the total bits and messages sent and received, and optionally the average round trip delay. Only standard open connections are counted, not measurement links, experimental NCP links or link 0. Another optional measurement is the distribution of message types on link 0.

The last 24 hour sample is made available by a process on a well-known socket (still to be specified) that supports ICP. Its message starts with a word holding a Day # and a start time in minutes, from 0 (midnight) to 1439. The next word holds the source host, byte size, number of host entries and a format byte whose bits say which statistics follow: message counts, byte counts, average round-trip time and control message distribution.
sections.plainLanguage: Every computer would keep a daily tally of how much it sent and got, and be ready to show the tally to anyone who asks, in an agreed layout.

sections.title: Other Measurement Ideas
sections.content:
R. Metcalfe suggested measuring connections as if they were commodities: capacity in bits per second, transmission delay, mean time between failures and percent availability. The first two are fairly easy; the last two are harder.

The RFC also describes HOST survey programs that periodically test whether HOSTs are up. The MIT/DMCG program does this every 15 minutes and records states coded 0 to 5, from "HOST not surveyed" to "Logger available". Details are in RFC 308.

Finally, the NWG wanted file transfer measurements and artificial traffic generators. At Lincoln Labs, J. Forgie kept traffic between 4800 bps and 38K bps; UCLA reached around 75K bps using multiple links in parallel.
sections.plainLanguage: They also wanted to check which computers were awake and to build a machine that makes pretend traffic, a bit like testing a road by driving lots of empty trucks on it.
